title: Singapore Launches New Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI
date_evidence: Visible byline 'DAVOS - 22 JAN 2026' and 'LAST UPDATED: 22 Jan 2026' on the IMDA press release page; also '22 Jan 2026|5 mins read' in the page header.
key_claim: On 22 January 2026 IMDA launched the Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI at the World Economic Forum in Davos, the first such framework worldwide, focused on four areas: assessing and bounding the risks upfront, making humans meaningfully accountable, implementing technical controls, and enabling end-user responsibility, with compliance voluntary but organisations remaining legally accountable for their agents' behaviours and actions.
frame_summary: Argues that AI agents acting on users' behalf require an explicit governance regime that bounds the agent's actions in advance, ties every action to an accountable human or organisation, and is delivered in advance of agent deployment, rather than retrofitted afterward.

title: How Agentic AI Will Reshape Payments (IMF Note 2026/004)
date_evidence: Visible byline on IMF page: 'By Sonja Davidovic, Herve Tourpe   April 24, 2026'; series ID 'IMF Notes No 2026/004', Stock No INSEA2026004.
key_claim: Agent-initiated payments challenge existing payment regimes because authorization stops being a per-transaction instruction from the account holder and becomes structural and mandate-based, raising unresolved questions about traceability, consent and liability under existing legal frameworks, and the IMF proposes a three-layer framework that keeps strict deterministic rule-based controls in the authorisation and settlement layers while agentic AI operates in an upstream intent and orchestration layer.
frame_summary: Argues the live tension is between probabilistic agentic AI and the deterministic payment-system rulebook, and that institutional design rather than technology will decide whether agentic payments preserve authorisation and finality.
verbatim_quote: Authorization instead becomes structural and mandate based, which raises questions about traceability, consent, and liability under existing legal frameworks.
cluster: When the Agent Signs: AI Agents Inside the Thai e-Transactions Perimeter
notes: Anchor for the authorization-traceability gap that the Thai ETA's electronic-signature and trust-services rules presume to be solved.

title: The Agentic AI Landscape and Its Conceptual Foundations (OECD AI Papers No. 56)
date_evidence: OECD AI Papers series catalogue: 'OECD ARTIFICIAL INTELLIGENCE PAPERS February 2026 No. 56 THE AGENTIC AI...'; release noted in OECD listing as 13 February 2026; DOI https://doi.org/10.1787/396cf758-en.
key_claim: The OECD paper attempts to define agentic AI for governance purposes by identifying the most frequently cited features in existing definitions and mapping them to the OECD definition of an AI system, and presents descriptive data on the recent uptake of AI agents and agentic AI across 177 countries, signalling that an authoritative international definition is being assembled for downstream regulation.
frame_summary: Argues that policymakers need a precise, shared concept of agentic AI before they can govern it, and the OECD is positioning itself as the international body that supplies that definition for downstream regulators to inherit.

title: AI Agents Could Be Worth $236 Billion by 2034 - If We Ensure They Are the Good Kind
date_evidence: Visible byline on WEF page: 'Jan 15, 2026'; meta-og:url confirms /stories/2026/01/ai-agents-trust/; article tagged 'World Economic Forum Annual Meeting 2026'.
key_claim: WEF proposes a Know Your Agent (KYA) framework alongside Know Your Customer, resting on four capabilities (establishing who the agent is, confirming what it is permitted to do and for whom, maintaining accountability for every action, continuously monitoring behaviour), and warns that agent identity is only as trustworthy as the underlying KYC: 'without high-assurance KYC, even the strongest KYA framework collapses', positioning identity-and-trust providers as the load-bearing layer of agentic commerce.
frame_summary: Argues that the existing KYC trust regime built for human-initiated transactions must be paired with a Know Your Agent regime layered on top of high-assurance identity, or agentic commerce will produce automated fraud at scale.
verbatim_quote: Agent identity is only as trustworthy as the underlying human or organizational identity it represents - without high-assurance KYC, even the strongest KYA framework collapses.
cluster: When the Agent Signs: AI Agents Inside the Thai e-Transactions Perimeter
notes: Directly relevant to ETDA's NDID consortium and the e-Signature certification mandate; KYA framing is being adopted by Visa and Mastercard.

title: Singapore Launches New Model AI Governance Framework for Agentic AI
date_evidence: Visible byline on Allen & Gledhill perspective page: '13 February 2026'; category 'Knowledge Highlights'.
key_claim: AI agents access sensitive data and can make changes to their environment, such as updating a customer database or making a payment, which 'may result in unauthorised or erroneous actions', and the increased autonomy creates 'challenges for effective human accountability, such as greater automation bias, or the tendency to over-trust an automated system that has performed reliably in the past', and IMDA's framework requires organisations to define 'significant checkpoints in the agentic workflow that require human approval, such as high-stakes or irreversible actions'.
frame_summary: Argues that the IMDA framework treats automation bias and the loss of meaningful human checkpoints as the central agentic-AI governance failure mode, and that organisations are accountable in advance for designing the checkpoints.
verbatim_quote: AI agents' access to sensitive data and ability to make changes to their environment, such as updating a customer database or making a payment, may, for example, result in unauthorised or erroneous actions.
cluster: When the Agent Signs: AI Agents Inside the Thai e-Transactions Perimeter
notes: Independent Singapore-counsel reading of the IMDA framework; uses 'making a payment' as the canonical example, directly relevant to Thai e-transactions and NDID.

title: Thailand's AI and Machine Learning Governance Framework for Capital Markets
date_evidence: Visible byline on Tilleke & Gibbins insight page: 'April 3, 2026' immediately above article title.
key_claim: Thailand's Securities and Exchange Commission has published a principle-based AI/ML governance framework for capital market business operators (securities and derivatives firms, asset managers, mutual and private fund managers, investment advisers including robo-advisory providers, derivatives intermediaries, market operators), structured around four core principles (fairness, legal and ethical compliance, accountability, transparency) and best practices across four AI/ML lifecycle stages, signalling supervisory expectations though currently nonbinding.
frame_summary: Argues Thailand's sectoral regulators are moving ahead with non-binding AI governance guidance keyed to lifecycle accountability, which sets the supervisory tone for ETDA and other Thai authorities even before the Thai AI Act is enacted.
verbatim_quote: The guidelines name four core principles for AI/ML deployment: Fairness... Legal and ethical compliance... Accountability... Transparency.

title: Trends: Agentic Commerce Next 'Inflection Point' in SE Asia's Digital Payments Landscape

key_claim: Agentic commerce, AI agents initiating, executing and reconciling payments through open APIs with little human intervention, is expected to become a regional reality across ASEAN within three years, riding the Regional Payment Connectivity initiative now signed by nine ASEAN central banks, with the primary concerns identified by industry as accountability: 'who handles fraud, chargebacks and post-transaction disputes when the human is removed from the chain'.
